source.title: Mathematical Models of Computation in Superposition
source.authors: Kaarel Hänni; Jake Mendel; Dmitry Vaintrob; Lawrence Chan

record.file_problem: The text is readable, with some PDF extraction artifacts; it is not cut off.
record.tranche_reason: The paper gives theoretical constructions and bounds for sparse features represented and computed in superposition, bearing on the toy-model superposition claim through a different task and analysis. It does not reproduce the original toy-model training or measure its sparsity-dependent transition.
record.gate_note: The paper's results are mathematical constructions and proofs, not experiments on trained models. Theorems about general sparse boolean circuits are not included separately unless they directly bear on the superposition representation claims. Cited empirical findings about language models and sparse autoencoders are not the paper's own results.
record.test_reason: This is a purely mathematical paper. It takes as given that sparse boolean features are encoded as almost-orthogonal directions, then proves that networks can compute boolean circuits (U-AND, sparse circuits, error correction) on them. It contains no trained networks and no measurement of whether small networks learn superposed geometry or a sparsity-dependent transition. The random-init result (Theorem 3) concerns untrained weights. These existence and representability results describe what a network could do, not whether V1's empirical claim holds. They are recorded under fits_no_version, not as tests.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors give constructions showing networks can compute sparse boolean circuits (U-AND, low-depth circuits, and deep circuits via error-correction layers) entirely in superposition. They argue random-init networks likely emulate U-AND, and flag limits: asymptotic results, binary features, a sparsity assumption, and the ε-linear representation choice.
record.recipe_differences: The original source studies toy models of feature storage; this paper gives mathematical constructions and random-weight results for computation of boolean circuits in superposition rather than reproducing the original training setup or measure.
record.method_sensitivity: The results depend on sparsity, input encoding (basis-aligned versus superposed), interference/error parameters, and, for Theorem 14, approximate input norm and Gaussian random weights.

fits_no_version.finding: Theorems 1–3 and 14 prove that one-layer MLPs can compute all pairwise ANDs of m sparse features with far fewer neurons than outputs, even with superposed inputs. Random Gaussian init suffices.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Computation in superposition: networks can compute many more sparse boolean features than neurons, not just store them.

fits_no_version.finding: Theorems 6 and 8 plus Lemma 7 (error correction) let deep networks of width d emulate sparse circuits of width Õ(d^1.5) at polynomial depth.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Deep sparse boolean circuits can be emulated entirely in superposition, given error-correction layers.

record.peer_reviewed: Presented in the inaugural Mechanistic Interpretability Workshop at ICML 2024
record.problems: Evidence is theoretical and asymptotic, not empirical evaluation of trained networks. The paper focuses on binary sparse features and does not test sparsity transitions, feature importance, or whether these constructions are used in real models.
record.rows_left_out: Theorems 6 and 8 also establish constructions for broader sparse boolean circuits, but their stated result is circuit emulation rather than a separately measured feature geometry or storage result relevant to V1.

untested.parts: Whether trained small networks store sparse features as nearly orthogonal directions, the sparsity-dependent transition, and the regular geometry. The paper assumes the encoding and proves computation results only.
The whole version. The authors only note that their model allows equally important features, unlike prior toy models.
The whole version. They discuss that probed features may be unused, but give no test of non-capacity polysemanticity.
The whole version. There are no LLM measurements; Gurnee et al. and SAE work are only cited.
The whole version. They argue for caution about whether SAE features are used, and suggest dictionaries of size around d², but test nothing.
The whole version. The binary 1-D features are an assumption; non-binary features are listed as a limitation.

record.verdict_notes: Theoretical paper only. The near-orthogonal feature encoding and sparsity are assumptions, so no result tests V1–V6. The interpretability takeaways (about d² feature capacity; probe-detectable features may be unused; SAE nonlinearity choices) are arguments, not tests. The reader's 'supports V1' label is removed.

versions.untested_parts: The paper does not test a sparsity-dependent transition, compare feature importance, or measure the prevalence of this geometry in trained networks. Its constructions establish particular representability results for sparse boolean inputs.
No test of capacity competition, dedicated dimensions for important features, or polysemantic neurons.
The paper discusses the possibility that a probed feature need not be used in computation, but does not test polysemantic neurons arising through other mechanisms.
No measurements of feature spread or SAE-recoverable features in LLMs.
No test of whether SAE features are complete, stable, or canonical.
The paper does not compare one-dimensional feature directions with multidimensional feature representations.

rows.subject: single-layer neural network
rows.operation_detail: Proved ε-linear representation of the Universal AND circuit on s-sparse, basis-aligned inputs.

conditions.value: all pairwise ANDs of m inputs

rows.measure: ε-linear representability of the Universal AND outputs
rows.baseline: Naive implementation uses one neuron per pairwise AND, requiring m choose 2 neurons.
rows.value: Theorem 1 states width d = Õ_m(1/ε²); the proof sketch gives d = Θ(log⁸ m/ε²) for error below ε.
rows.note: An existence result for sparse-input computation; it does not measure a learned representation or a sparsity transition.
rows.check: This is an existence proof (Theorem 1) for a hand-constructed MLP computing pairwise ANDs, not a measurement of how a trained network stores features. It bears on computation in superposition, which no listed version names. The baseline is the paper's naive construction, not a control.

rows.subject: single-layer neural network
rows.size_stated: input size and width d = Õ(√m/ε²)
rows.operation_detail: Proved ε-linear representation of the Universal AND circuit from inputs encoded in superposition.

conditions.value: features encoded by almost-orthogonal unit-norm vectors

rows.measure: ε-linear representability of the Universal AND outputs
rows.value: Theorem 2 states that such a network exists with width d = Õ(√m/ε²); the feature encoding uses almost-orthogonal unit-norm vectors.
rows.note: The result establishes a construction with inputs in superposition, rather than an empirical geometry measurement.
rows.check: This is a constructive proof (Theorem 2). The almost-orthogonal input encoding is chosen by the authors as an assumption, not observed in a network, so it cannot bear on V1's geometry claim.

rows.subject: one-layer MLP with randomly initialized weights
rows.operation_detail: Proved ε-linear representability of the Universal AND circuit for weights drawn i.i.d. from a Gaussian distribution.

conditions.value: Win entries drawn i.i.d. from N(0, δ²)

rows.measure: ε-linear representability of the Universal AND outputs
rows.value: Theorem 3 states that the MLP ε-linearly represents the circuit outside negligible probability.
rows.uncertainty: negligible-probability guarantee; no numerical probability stated
rows.note: This is a theoretical result about random weights, not a result about training or how often networks use the represented features.
rows.check: This is a theorem about randomly initialized, untrained Gaussian weights. It shows the network represents ANDs; it does not show learned superposition.

rows.subject: one-layer ReLU network with random Gaussian weight matrix
rows.operation_detail: Proved that pairwise AND features are ε-linearly represented after a ReLU layer, with an almost-orthogonal collection of output feature vectors.

conditions.value: approximately radius r, with r² = Õ(s)

rows.measure: Pairwise AND feature representability and output feature interference
rows.value: Theorem 14 gives ε(1) = Õ(max(sμ, sε, √(s/d))) and μ(1) = Õ(max(1/√d, μ)); the output feature vectors form an almost-orthogonal collection.
rows.uncertainty: outside negligible probability; no numerical probability stated
rows.note: The authors state the result asymptotically and require approximately norm-controlled inputs. It does not test a transition across sparsity levels.
rows.check: This is an appendix theorem (Theorem 14) with an assumed near-orthogonal input encoding and random weights. The output almost-orthogonality is a proved property of the construction, not a measured geometry of a trained model.

reader_labels.condition: Theoretical constructions for sparse inputs, including inputs encoded in superposition
reader_labels.reason: The results establish sparse-input pairwise-AND representations in widths below the number of outputs, and Theorems 2 and 14 describe almost-orthogonal feature encodings or output feature vectors (r1–r4).
